briefing: Iran says talks are under way on a plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if Washington meets its terms, after a letter from U.S. Vice-President JD Vance that Tehran called a change in tone; oil still ended October up about 14%. Americans vote Tuesday with more than 44 million ballots already cast and the Senate a toss-up, and Ottawa tables its budget Thursday. Clocks in Ontario fall back one hour at 2 a.m. Sunday.

stories.backstory: The U.S. and Israel began striking Iran on Feb. 28, and Iran responded by choking traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil. A June peace memorandum briefly reopened the strait, but it collapsed in July and the U.S. imposed a blockade on Iranian shipping. Yemen's Houthis have since widened the fight with missile attacks on Saudi Arabia, and Egypt's parliament has authorized sending troops to help the Saudis. Qatar handed Iran a new draft deal on Oct. 25, which Tehran said contained ideas it could not accept.
stories.headline: Iran says talks under way on two-day plan to reopen Hormuz
stories.impact: Expect GTA gas and diesel prices to stay high, which feeds into grocery, delivery and transit costs. Alberta oil revenues rise, but Ontario households and manufacturers mostly feel the cost side.
stories.now: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said talks with Qatari mediators are under way on a plan to reopen the strait within two days, provided Washington accepts Tehran's conditions. Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei said a letter from U.S. Vice-President JD Vance showed a markedly changed tone, which he called a positive sign. Separately, Iran's Revolutionary Guard navy said more tankers caught fire after hitting mines on what it calls unauthorized routes, and Oman evacuated injured crew from an attacked vessel; these claims have not been confirmed by maritime authorities. On Friday the expiring December Brent contract settled at US$117.64, while the January contract, now the benchmark, closed at US$113.43, up about 14% for October; U.S. WTI closed at US$104.12.

stories.why: Oil above US$110 is the main force behind higher inflation in Canada and the U.S., and it pushed the Bank of Canada into a rate hike this week. A real reopening plan could pull prices down quickly, while a collapse of talks could send them higher.

stories.backstory: Broad Canada-U.S. trade talks collapsed in August, and Trump then imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion of Canadian goods, prompting Canadian counter-tariffs. Since then the White House has repeatedly adjusted which products are covered, easing some farm and forestry goods while adding others. Separate U.S. tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos under a national-security law (Section 232) hit Ontario's factories hardest. Sources said this week a narrower deal on steel and autos was possible before the midterms, but U.S. officials want more concessions.
stories.headline: Carney widens trade push as U.S. deal stays out of reach
stories.impact: Factory jobs in Windsor, Oshawa, Hamilton and the GTA's parts plants remain exposed. Some imported goods such as paint, rugs and air conditioners may cost more if Canada responds or suppliers pass on costs.
stories.now: From Oct. 30, the U.S. dropped plywood, plastic wrap, cardboard boxes and some food machinery from its 50% tariff list on Canadian goods but added items including cocoa powder, paint, fibreboard (MDF), carpets and rugs, air conditioners and canoes. Talks with Washington have intensified without a breakthrough, and Trump has said steel and auto tariffs on Canada will rise to 50% on Jan. 1. Ottawa is leaning on other markets: a new partnership with the United Arab Emirates this week, a Canada-EU summit in Montreal, a trip to Antigua and Barbuda Nov. 2–4, and India's envoy saying a trade deal could be ready before Prime Minister Narendra Modi visits Dec. 11–12. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says Canadians need results, not signing ceremonies.

stories.why: Ontario sells most of its steel and auto output to the U.S., and the province says steel exports there have fallen by more than half since 2024. The midterm result could change how willing Washington is to bargain.

stories.backstory: Ontario's spring budget had already forecast a deficit near $13.8 billion as U.S. tariffs hit steel and auto exports. The province's steel exports to the U.S. fell to $4.1 billion in the first eight months of 2026 from $8.4 billion in the same period of 2024. Ottawa and Ontario announced an $8.7-billion action plan for steel, autos and critical minerals in October. The legislature returned on Oct. 27 after a 21-week break.
stories.headline: Ontario deficit grows to $16.9 billion; balance pushed to 2029-30
stories.impact: Most homes use about 700 kWh a month, so the rebate cap mainly affects heavy electricity users from May 2027. Businesses investing in equipment get faster write-offs, and buyers of newly built homes keep the HST break.
stories.now: Thursday's fall economic statement projects a $16.9-billion deficit for 2026-27, up from $13.8 billion in the spring budget, followed by shortfalls of $12.7 billion and $6.7 billion before a $200-million surplus in 2029-30. The province now expects growth of just 0.5% this year and 1.5% in 2027, with unemployment at 7.2% this year. New and confirmed measures include an $8-billion business write-off matching Ottawa's, about $8 billion more for health care by decade's end, and a nearly $4-billion top-up to the contingency fund for more tariffs. The Ontario Electricity Rebate will be capped at 1,200 kWh a month for homes starting May 2027, and the $4-billion Protect Ontario Investment Fund is paused. Opposition parties called the update weak on affordability.

stories.summary: Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy's fall update raised this year's deficit by more than $3 billion and delayed a balanced budget by a year as the trade war slows growth.
stories.why: A bigger deficit and slower growth limit room for new programs and tax relief, and confirm the trade war is hurting Ontario more than other provinces.

stories.backstory: The Bank of Canada cut to 2.25% in October 2025 and then held for seven meetings. Oil prices driven up by the Iran war lifted September inflation to 3.1%, even as Canada lost 68,000 jobs that month. The bank's new forecast puts 2027 inflation at 3.1%, well above its 2% target. Flat growth and rising rates together raise the risk of stagflation, meaning weak growth with high inflation.
stories.headline: Economy stalls in August, two days after Bank of Canada's hike
stories.impact: Variable-rate mortgages and lines of credit already cost more after the hike. A weak economy could slow hiring in the GTA, so it is a good moment to review budgets and renewal plans.
stories.now: Real gross domestic product (GDP) was unchanged in August, missing the 0.2% gain economists expected, with retail up 1.2% but wholesale trade and car-and-parts manufacturing down. StatCan's early estimate shows a 0.1% drop in September as manufacturing and oil and gas output fell, leaving third-quarter growth at about 0.3%. That follows Wednesday's quarter-point hike to 2.50%, which the Bank of Canada made to keep high oil prices from spreading through the economy, while signalling more could be needed. Premier Doug Ford called the hike a massive mistake, and Ontario's fall update now sees provincial growth of only 0.5% this year.

stories.backstory: Republicans have held both chambers of Congress since January 2025. All 435 House seats and about a third of the Senate are on the ballot on Nov. 3. Tariffs and high gas prices tied to the Iran war have hurt Trump's approval, which Reuters recently put at 32%. Recent national polls have given Democrats a lead on the generic ballot.
stories.headline: Early vote passes 44 million as midterms enter final weekend
stories.impact: The outcome will shape U.S. tariff policy on Canadian steel and autos and the timing of any strikes on Iran, both of which affect Ontario jobs and fuel prices.
stories.now: About 44.8 million Americans had voted by Thursday evening, according to the University of Florida Election Lab, well ahead of the 2022 pace; early turnout in Texas is up about 50%. Democrats lead the RealClearPolling generic-ballot average 51.4% to 43.2%, and analysts call a House flip likely while the Senate stays uncertain. CBS News rates Maine, Michigan, Ohio, Texas and Alaska as Senate toss-ups, and an Emerson poll has Democrat Adam Hamilton ahead of Sen. Roger Marshall 49% to 45% in Kansas. Trump plans in-person rallies in Iowa and Kansas on Sunday plus tele-rallies in 19 states.

stories.backstory: The attack drew national attention because it took place in the Bridle Path, one of Toronto's wealthiest neighbourhoods. The family's father, David Morton, CEO of MAC Group, has called the experience terrifying and urged anyone with information to come forward. Police say it was the 119th home invasion reported in Toronto this year, up about 32% from the same period in 2025. Chief Myron Demkiw promised a stronger police presence in the area.
stories.headline: Canada-wide warrant issued in Bridle Path home invasion
stories.impact: Police remain on the lookout for two more suspects in their 20s, so North York residents may see extra patrols. Police are asking anyone with information or home security video from the area to contact them.
stories.now: Police issued a Canada-wide arrest warrant on Saturday for Daijohn Richards, 23, who went to hospital later on Oct. 29 with a gunshot wound to the shoulder that police believe another suspect fired by accident. He faces charges including discharging a firearm with intent to wound, armed robbery and aggravated assault. Police say three masked men with handguns and a hammer forced their way into a Hyde Park Circle home near Bayview and Lawrence avenues around 3:45 a.m.; three of the four family members were shot and two were struck with a hammer. All four are expected to survive, though two have life-altering injuries, and police believe the home was chosen for the area's wealth rather than the family itself.

stories.backstory: The Fed raised rates in September for the first time in three years as the Iran war pushed oil above US$100 a barrel. Tech giants have spent heavily on artificial intelligence (AI), and those stocks have driven much of the market's swings this month. Strong U.S. growth paired with high energy prices keeps pressure on the Fed not to cut.
stories.headline: U.S. economy grows 3.4% in third quarter as inflation cools
stories.impact: Canadian fixed mortgage rates follow bond yields, so they are unlikely to fall soon. Strong U.S. demand helps Ontario exporters that are not hit by tariffs.
stories.now: The Bureau of Economic Analysis said real GDP grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter, up from 2.2% in the second, driven by business investment in equipment and computers, inventory building and consumer spending. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index rose at a 2.1% rate, down from 5.0%, and core PCE, which excludes food and energy, eased to 2.5%. The data came a day after the Federal Reserve held its key rate at 3.75% to 4% in a 10-2 vote, with Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack favouring a hike. Gold fell to a one-year low on Friday as investors bet rates will stay high.

stories.backstory: Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, so voters can rank both Sullivans. Peltola, a former congresswoman, is seen as a serious challenger to the incumbent. Trump has called for Peltola to be prosecuted, and it is unusual for prosecutors to confirm an investigation this close to a vote. A federal appeals court recently refused a similar Justice Department request to set aside about 20,000 California ballots.
stories.headline: Federal prosecutors open criminal probe in Alaska Senate race
stories.impact: Little direct effect on Ontario, but a disputed or delayed Senate result could prolong uncertainty over U.S. trade policy toward Canada.
stories.now: U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman confirmed a months-long investigation and a surge of federal law-enforcement resources to Alaska, but did not name targets or possible crimes. It follows a New York Times report that Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign appeared to help recruit retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan, who shares a name with Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan; Peltola and the second Sullivan both deny it. In a separate civil case, the Justice Department wants ballots ranking the second Sullivan set aside and has asked a judge to rule by Monday. Alaska's lawyers say the ballot already tells the two men apart.

stories.backstory: The Justice Department sued California on Oct. 15, alleging that more than 20,000 registered voters are likely noncitizens. U.S. elections are run by states, and the Constitution gives them primary control over how they are held. The administration has pressed several states over voter rolls ahead of the midterms.
stories.headline: Courts block Trump bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots
stories.impact: Little direct effect in Ontario, but disputes over vote counting could delay results in close races that decide control of Congress.
stories.now: A three-judge panel of the 9th Circuit ruled 2-1 on Friday that setting the ballots aside would violate the Constitution's Elections Clause and risk disenfranchising eligible voters, with Judge Patrick Bumatay dissenting. Late Friday, U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson issued a temporary restraining order barring federal officials from demanding that California officials separate or withhold ballots, or threatening them with prosecution. The Justice Department has also sent letters to all 50 states telling them to preserve election records for 22 months.

stories.backstory: Canada joined the EU's SAFE defence procurement program in February as Ottawa looked to diversify away from the U.S. A Canada-EU trade deal (CETA) has been in force provisionally since 2017. The term 'associate member' was dropped from a draft statement days before the summit. Carney also visited the United Arab Emirates this month to expand trade ties.
stories.headline: Canada and EU launch 'Alliance for the Future' and aim for associate ties
stories.impact: Nothing changes right away, but over time it could open more European markets to Ontario firms and widen work and study options for young people.
stories.now: Carney and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen launched an 'Alliance for the Future' focused on AI, energy, critical minerals and quantum technology. Both backed the idea of Canada as the EU's first 'associate' member, though the final joint statement used the phrase 'ever-closer association' after some member states asked for more time. Carney said the substance will be worked out in coming months, plans to attend a June meeting of European leaders, and the sides aim to define the concept by the 2027 summit. He said it could make it easier for young Canadians to live, study and travel in Europe.

stories.backstory: Israelis voted on Oct. 27 amid an eight-month war with Iran that has reshaped regional politics. Netanyahu's outgoing coalition held 60 seats when the last Knesset dissolved in July. Arab parties won more seats than in any previous election, making them potential kingmakers.
stories.headline: Final count leaves Netanyahu's bloc at 53 seats, short of a majority
stories.impact: Indirect for Ontario, mainly through oil prices and the wider conflict's effect on inflation.
stories.now: Final results give Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc 53 of 120 seats and the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot 48, with Arab-led parties holding the balance. Likud figures alleged fraud, but the Central Elections Committee said the vote was lawful and there was no basis for claims of election theft. The Joint List said it is ready to help form an alternative government, and Ra'am leader Mansour Abbas said he has talked with both sides. Results are due to be certified on Nov. 4, after which President Isaac Herzog consults parties.

stories.backstory: Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, and both sides now regularly strike each other's energy sites. A local humanitarian ceasefire began in occupied Oleshky in Kherson region on Oct. 27, and a Ukrainian delegation arrived there on Oct. 30. U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff met Putin on Oct. 21 as Washington pushes for new talks.
stories.headline: Russian strike cuts power in parts of Kyiv as Canada pledges €500 million
stories.impact: Canada's €500-million pledge adds to federal spending ahead of Thursday's budget; the war also keeps European energy markets tight, adding to global fuel prices.
stories.now: A Russian strike hit an energy facility in Kyiv on Saturday, leaving parts of the city without electricity and water. Canada pledged 500 million euros toward an international support loan as Ukraine faces a 2027 budget gap, following large pledges from Norway and the U.K. Earlier the U.S. approved the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles, though President Zelensky warned deliveries may take years, and Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Moscow's position is unchanged. Zelensky hopes for three-way talks with the U.S. in Abu Dhabi between Nov. 6 and 10.

stories.backstory: Weekend closures have become routine as Metrolinx builds out GO Expansion and the TTC does track and signal work. This weekend's closures overlap with Halloween events and the end of daylight saving time at 2 a.m. Sunday.
stories.headline: Subway, GO and UP Express closures hit Halloween weekend
stories.impact: Leave extra time for trips downtown or to Pearson this weekend, and check TTC and GO service alerts before heading out.
stories.now: The TTC has no Line 2 Bloor-Danforth service between St. George and Broadview stations this weekend, with shuttle buses running instead. Metrolinx has no Barrie line trains between Downsview Park and Union on Oct. 31 and Nov. 1, so riders are told to use Line 1, and UP Express service to and from Pearson airport is suspended for the weekend. Kitchener line riders face construction-related bus replacements, and some Stouffville line trains are running late or replaced by buses.

stories.backstory: Toronto uses traffic agents to direct vehicles at busy intersections near construction zones and during rush hour. The Thorncliffe Park area around Millwood and Overlea sees heavy truck traffic. Careless driving causing death is a provincial offence, not a Criminal Code charge.
stories.headline: Dump truck driver charged after Toronto traffic agent killed
stories.impact: Drivers in construction zones should watch for traffic agents and follow their directions; expect continued scrutiny of turning trucks in dense neighbourhoods.
stories.now: Police say a southbound dump truck turning left from Millwood Road onto Overlea Boulevard hit the 42-year-old agent around 9 a.m. Thursday, and he died at the scene. The 33-year-old driver stayed and co-operated, and was charged with careless driving causing death under the Highway Traffic Act. He is due in court on Jan. 28, and police are asking for dashcam or security video. Mayor Olivia Chow identified the victim later Thursday.
